translations.text: Another account of Saint Mar Jacob, the divine teacher and bishop of Batnan of Serugh.
This saint’s father was from Kurtam, on the Euphrates River. His mother was barren, and her husband brought her to Mar of Bar-Hadath.
They prayed there, and, according to God’s will, he had relations with her, and she gave birth to a marvelous son.
When he was three years old, his parents brought him there to pray on the day commemorating Mar Muqim. The little child was there while a large crowd stood there and the place was full of priests.
When the Holy Spirit moved to descend and consecrate the body of our life-giver, our Lord and God and Savior Jesus Christ, that child stirred and climbed down from his mother’s lap.
He made his way through the people standing in God’s house, went up into the holy sanctuary, and stood before the table of life, while everyone in the martyrs’ shrine watched him.
The angel of the Lord moved and gave him God’s gift. He stretched out his hands and drank three handfuls, like Ezekiel when he ate the scroll.
From that moment the Spirit of the Lord came mightily upon him, and he began to utter speech that was not that of someone awake. He was brought up in Hawra of Serugh.
He became a visiting priest there and composed many hymns there. The Spirit called him and made him a shepherd in the church of Batnan of Serugh.
He wrote compositions and interpretations, as well as histories, dialogue hymns, and glorious teaching free from error. His Lord found rest and took his rest in him.
We have found that his teaching amounts to fifty [?] in extent, and the homilies number seven hundred and sixty-three.
There were also other hymns, which he did not finish, about Mary and Golgotha. This Mar Jacob lived in the time of Mar Severus the patriarch. He went up to him and received his blessing.
He went up in a procession of many bishops from all over the East.

As for the conduct of Saint Mar Jacob—his chastity, holiness, purity, ascetic discipline, vigils, toil, weariness, service, weeping, sighs, love, virtue, and prayers—we have too little time to recount them down to the day of his death.
May his prayer and supplication be a wall and a refuge for us at all times, forever and ever. Amen.
The account of Mar Jacob is finished. Strength was in that man, and he broke his bonds, escaped from them, and went and told those villages what he had seen.
When they heard, they came and found the monastery empty and the saint’s bones taken away. They raised a great lament and gnashed their teeth, saying:

“Who has done this to you?” That man showed them the road by which they had gone. Two hundred horsemen from among them made ready and pursued them as far as the village of Danbuth, in the territory of Amida.

When they saw them on the road, before coming near them, they planned to kill them. When they caught up with them, they drew their swords, but before they could reach them, they were struck with convulsions, from the [?] to the eldest, both they and their leaders, until they could no longer recognize the road.
When this happened to them, they realized that this event was from God.
They began pleading, saying, “We beg you, our lords, release us so that we can go back along the road. Take the holy bones yourselves and go in peace from now on,
“for this event is from God.” But those monks did not yield to their pleading. They remained in torment all that night until morning.
In the morning, when they saw those wretched men suffering, they felt pity for them [?] and said to them, “What do you want?” They answered, “Release us so that we can go.”
They prayed to God for them, and they were healed. They approached, and two of them approached the monks and said to them, “Forgive us this offense,
“and give us a portion of the saint’s bones, so that we may not be deprived of his prayers.”
This pleased the monks, and they extended their right hands to them, prayed over them, and greeted them with peace. He said to them, “Go in peace; return to your own country.”

They rejoiced greatly and asked the blessed Romanus for permission to return to their monastery and their honored position, and he granted it. They returned with them, having promised that they would not [?]. When they [?] Nisibis,
they sent messengers to the blessed Hura to announce their arrival.
When the blessed man heard that they had come, he rejoiced greatly and went out to meet them. Before they met one another, Saint Mar Hura wanted them to place Saint Mar Aha in the lower monastery.

When they reached the crossroads, the mule carrying the coffin broke its tether and ran headlong. They could not restrain it until it reached the gate of the upper monastery. It cried out, and the blessed Abraham of Kokab heard it and recognized it.

He went out to meet it. When he saw the mule, he rejoiced greatly, approached, and received a blessing from the saint’s body. He brought the mule inside, lowered the coffin before the altar, opened it, and pressed his eyes against the bones of the blessed Mar Aha.

He said, “My father, where is the monastery’s former [?]? Instead of the innocent lambs that were in it, look, it has become a dwelling for destructive wolves; and instead of the songs and praises that used to be heard in it,

there is the sound of leopards and lions roaring for destruction.” While the blessed man was lamenting these things, the blessed Hura and his companions entered, fell down before the saint’s bones, and received a blessing from them.

All the blessed men sat down together and wrote letters to all the brothers, wherever they had been scattered from the monastery, announcing the news of the saint’s bones. They gathered from wherever they were.
Their number came to about one hundred and twenty brothers. They held a great vigil that day, on the first of October, and the blessed Hura provided them with food and drink.
He brought out money of his own and distributed it to them as gifts. He also bought us another five teams of oxen and gave them to them.
He gave them a great deal of grain, and they sowed good seed. They restored the vineyard of the upper monastery and the orchard of the lower monastery,

as well as the woodland beside the river, and repaired its mill. The Lord prospered them with abundant and plentiful crops, and that region was blessed through the bones of Saint Mar Aha. Never again did hail

fall in that region. They reaped the harvest of the lower monastery and went up to the upper monastery. The blessed Hura saw that the vineyards and fruit trees were very fine, and he rejoiced greatly over them.

He went up onto the monastery roof and looked [?] around it, and his soul rejoiced. He said to the brothers who had gathered beside him, “This monastery has been restored.” For this reason it has been called the Monastery of the Restoration to this day.
A portion of the cross arrived, and likewise the bones of Saint Mar Aha. After the bones of the blessed Mar Aha had arrived, the illustrious Mar Abraham went and built a monastery east of Hisn Kayfa,
on the bank of the River Tigris. He also named it the Monastery of the Cross, after the monastery of Benael.

It supplied what the first monastery of Benael lacked. Each year they sowed wheat, barley, and other crops there and brought them to the monastery of Benael. Since the brothers had become numerous and there were many dwellings in the monastery of Benael,

Mar Abraham and Mar Hura decreed that all the income of the monastery on the River Tigris, together with votive offerings, tithes, and any charitable gift anyone might give, should be kept and given to the monastery of Benael, because it was the foundation of all the monasteries.
The monastery grew greatly, and its glory became greater than before. It had many possessions and abundant crops, and there were three hundred brothers in it who bore its burdens.
However, many villages in that region, which is called Beth Gogai, had fallen into ruin during the monastery’s abandonment. The blessed Mar Hura had grown old and advanced in years.
He too made himself a small burial chamber with his own hands. He made three stone coffins in it, fitted them together, and made lids for them.

When he had grown old, his eyes had become too dim to see, and he had fallen mortally ill, he sent for all his brothers. He instructed and admonished them to preserve their monastic way of life in complete fear of God, with humility, fasting, and prayer,
and not to give the devil any opportunity to lead them astray. He brought out everything he owned and gave it to them, so that there would be no dispute among them.

He summoned Elijah of Besaya and appointed him their head. He admonished him, put him under oath, and instructed him not to exalt himself over his brothers, but to lead them in complete purity and holiness.
All those brothers were distressed over his death. They all gathered, and while they were speaking with him, he sank into that eternal sleep on the twenty-third of November.
They mourned him deeply, embalmed him with myrrh, and carried him in with great honor.
They wrapped him in fine cloths and fragrant spices and laid him in the tomb he had built for himself, in its eastern burial niche.
He departed from this world with a good name and upright conduct. He lived in this world peacefully and pleasantly, and not a single day did he stumble; and deprivation
he never knew. From the day he went out and entered the city [?] until his death, he did not return to their village, nor did he enter a city or even a single village.
He did not even eat bread outside his monastery, nor did he lie down to sleep outside it. His [?] was always prepared for every traveler, and his bowl [?]
was mixed, and he enjoyed the company of everyone who came and went.

And to people [?] beggars; rather, his table was the same for rich and poor, and his dealings with all people were the same. And in the world [?] and for the poor [?] to come, he stored up delights and eternal life for himself.
David’s first psalm was fulfilled in him, where it pronounces blessed the man who has not walked in the way of the wicked.
He meditated on the Lord’s law day and night, so that he might be like a tree planted beside the water, which puts out leaves and yields fruit in its season.
He began and completed his way of life according to the will of our Lord Jesus Christ and of his worshipful, holy Father,
and of his living and life-giving Spirit, to whom belong glory, honor, worship, splendor, and exaltation.
May he make us worthy of pardon for our debts and forgiveness of our sins through the prayers of Mary, who bore God, the mother of life and light,
and of the illustrious athlete, clothed in victory, Mar Aha, and of the holy, God-clothed [?] Hura,

and of the exalted Mar Michael, and of their entire blessed company, and of all who distinguished themselves before Christ through beautiful deeds of virtue. Amen. It is finished, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ. [?]
Everyone [?] who loves Christ and reads or comes upon these lines [?] should say to God, “In your mercy, forgive the one who wrote this account [?] of Mar Aha.”
And not [?] of body and spirit; and as [?] his lips utter, may he receive a reward. Amen.
